cells.tense: You are tending what you're growing, and you're doing it without forcing anything.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're tending and carry it this week until it needs nothing more from you. Notice what accepting that finish costs you.
cells.core:
You've got something growing that you're looking after well. Not smothering it, not cutting it back to keep it safe — giving it what it needs and letting it take the shape it takes. That's harder than either extreme.

The noise about whether it's done yet isn't running. You can work on a thing for an hour without the hour needing to add up to anything. There's a kind of finish here that isn't a defeat. You put the tool down, the thing is complete, and the completion is the point — not a flag to raise. Nobody has to notice for it to be real. Keep going at this pace and you'll end up with something lasting that didn't wear you down to make.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending something that's growing, and nothing about it is forced.
cells.verb: tending what you're growing through a form you keep choosing
cells.place: the solitary bench where repetition turns intention into skill

cells.tense: You are working ahead of the thing, forcing a harvest that hasn't ripened yet.
cells.ask: Stop one project while it's still good, before it's finished or fixed. Close the lid and walk away. Watch what your hands do for the rest of the hour.
cells.core:
You're tending something, but you're tending it past what it needs. Every session turns into a test of whether it's working, and the work gets buried under that question. Being good isn't enough — it has to prove it's getting somewhere, and prove it soon.

That proving is what's eating the thing. You're rehearsing the result while you're still making it. The schedule stops being a way to show up and starts being a way to check. And you keep at it, so the thing gets no room to just grow — it has to produce.

Pull back on one of them. Wanting it and pressuring it aren't the same thing, and you can put one down without losing the other. What you're doing is fine. It's the proving you can set aside.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending what's growing, but you're forcing the harvest before it's ripe.

cells.tense: You had a practice that was yours, and you stopped showing up to it.
cells.ask: Set your tools out tonight, whether or not you use them. Then sit with them for ten minutes with nothing else going on.
cells.core:
There was something you were tending — something you did because it was yours, with nothing productive attached to it. You can still see what it looked like when you were doing it well. The bench is sitting there and you're not on it.

Not that you don't care — you're just not in the room with the thing you care about. That's where you're standing, and I can't tell you how you got here. Your tools are where you left them. Set them out. Using them is a separate question from whether they're yours, and either answer is fine tonight. It doesn't have to be a big return, and it doesn't have to go well.

cells.tense: You are doing the work every day, and you are calling it something other than yours.
cells.ask: Say plainly what one of your daily practices actually gives you — one sentence, spoken to someone or written where you can see it.
cells.core:
You're showing up and doing the daily thing. You just don't count it. It's maintenance, it's habit, it's what you've done for years. Those aren't descriptions of the work — they're ways of not claiming it.

The care is real. People get fed by it, held by it, taught something by it, and the one doing the making is the one not getting credit. If someone said out loud what you do, you'd hear it as politeness.

This is small and it might feel like fussing. Say what the practice gives you. Not to a crowd — once is enough. After that, whether it's finished stops mattering as much.
cells.sheetLine: You're doing the work, and you're calling it habit instead of yours.

attempts.check: The record doesn't say the person was ever discouraged or stopped, so the Too Little cell can only locate them at the bench, not name what closed the door. A reader might rightly object that they show up every day and simply have a lot on, so the Too Much cell names only the widening schedule and the proof-seeking, not a verdict about who they are. Every ask survives a wrong read: carrying one thing to the point it needs nothing, stopping a project while it's still good, setting out tools without using them, and naming what a practice actually gives you are all useful to someone the card misread. The sentence that would serve the writer rather than the person is any line about the small steady light of their practice being holy, or the quiet bench being sacred — drop both.
